title: Residual Context Diffusion Language Models
one_liner: Diffusion models that decode many words at once waste computation by throwing away uncertain words, but recycling their hidden information fixes that.
lead: Most language models guess one word at a time. Diffusion models try to guess many words all at once, which finishes in fewer steps because multiple positions are refined in parallel, but they throw away the uncertain guesses instead of learning from them. This paper shows that the discarded guesses still contain useful context about what words should come next, because even uncertain predictions reveal patterns about neighboring words and the overall meaning, and proposes a way to recycle that context into the next refinement step, making the model faster and more accurate without adding much extra computation.

problem.h2: Throwing away information to go faster
paras: Normal language models (like ChatGPT) generate text one word at a time. A newer approach called diffusion language models works differently: they start with noise and refine many words at once in each step, like a blurry image gradually sharpening. This lets them finish in fewer steps because they are working on multiple words in parallel.

But these models have a flaw. At each step, the model is more confident about some words and less confident about others. The standard approach throws away the low-confidence words (the remasking trick), keeping only the confident ones for the next step. The low-confidence words are discarded completely, wasting the computation and the contextual information they contained.

callout.b: The waste: discarded words still know something useful about the context, but that knowledge is thrown out.
callout.html: Recycle the discarded words by converting their hidden information into residuals (adjustments) that feed into the next decoding step.

steps.text: Instead of discarding weak predictions, convert their hidden information into residuals (small numerical adjustments).

steps.text: Feed the adjustments into the model as additional context for the next denoising iteration.

object.h2: What the paper changes: discarded word information
paras: The paper changes one key thing: instead of throwing away the hidden numerical patterns from low-confidence predictions, it converts them into residual adjustments (small numerical corrections) and passes those adjustments to the next refinement step. This is a concrete, mechanical change to how the model recycles its intermediate computations.

hidden.name: contextual residuals (recycled adjustment signals)
paras: A contextual residual is the useful information hidden inside a low-confidence word that would normally be thrown away. It is not the word itself but the learned numerical pattern (vector) that the model produced while thinking about that word. Instead of deleting it, the paper converts that pattern into a small adjustment signal.

The paper measures and uses this by taking the hidden vectors of discarded words, passing them through a lightweight learned module, and adding the resulting adjustments back into the model's state before the next denoising step. This lets subsequent steps benefit from the context that the discarded words had already started to encode.

heat.caption: Darker residuals carry more contextual information; marked ones are recycled into next step.

reads.html: Residuals are the leftovers from discarded words—fragments of context that still have signal.
RCD extracts residual vectors from words (predictions) below the confidence threshold and injects them as contextual augmentation into the next denoising iteration.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: recycling computation preserves continuity
paras: Normally, discarding a word means its hidden information vanishes. The next step of refinement has no memory of it. But that discarded word had already begun to encode useful context—what words came before, what makes sense in this situation. By converting the discarded word's hidden representation into a residual adjustment, the paper preserves that partial understanding and smuggles it forward.

The next refinement step receives not just the kept words and fresh noise, but also these contextual hints. Because the hints are small adjustments rather than full new words, they act as guides without overwhelming the model's own predictions. The model learns to blend the carried-forward context with its fresh reasoning, making better decisions overall. This is efficient because the residuals are just numbers, which cost far less computation than recomputing the context from scratch, and the training uses two separate stages to avoid memory overload.

charts.title: Standard diffusion model (with remasking)
charts.note: Wastes computation on discarded words; throws away their context.

charts.title: With Residual Context Diffusion
charts.note: Recycles discarded words by carrying their contextual information forward, which lets the model make more informed decisions in later steps; on the hardest problems this nearly doubles accuracy and also needs 4-5 times fewer refinement iterations to reach baseline performance.

items.b: Residuals can drift too far from reality.
items.html: If the learned transformation W is not trained correctly, the injected residuals can mislead the next step instead of guiding it. This requires careful tuning of the two-stage training pipeline.

items.b: Memory still required during initial training.
items.html: The decoupled two-stage approach helps reduce memory later, but training the transformation layer initially still demands significant graphics-card memory because both the model and the learned transform must fit together before they can be split apart.

items.b: Residuals may not transfer across different model sizes or architectures.
items.html: A transformation trained on one model size may not work well when applied to a larger or differently-structured diffusion model.

items.b: Done right: residuals act as gentle contextual nudges.
items.html: When the learned transformation is trained properly on realistic data, the residuals improve both speed and accuracy because they carry true contextual information forward without overriding or confusing the model's own predictions.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small diffusion language model that decodes 8 words at each step. Implement standard remasking (discard low-confidence words) and compare it to RCD (convert discarded words to residuals and inject them). On a simple task like completing sentences or solving arithmetic problems, measure accuracy and count the total number of denoising steps needed to reach a target quality.
demo.metric_eq: improvement = (accuracy_with_RCD - accuracy_baseline) / accuracy_baseline * 100%, speed_gain = steps_baseline / steps_with_RCD
demo.closing: The demo must show that recycled residuals improve accuracy on the same number of steps, or reach baseline accuracy in fewer steps, proving that the discarded words genuinely carried forward useful context, because if residuals were just noise they would not consistently steer the model toward better predictions.
